title: Retconning the Curriculum: Why the Science of Learning Has a Serious Design Problem
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Hendrick argues that retrieval practice and spacing, though robustly supported by cognitive science, are increasingly misapplied in classrooms as bolt-on activities rather than curriculum properties. Using the TV trope of 'retconning,' he compares the awkward grafting of quizzes and mini-whiteboard reviews onto curricula never designed for them to poorly planned narrative twists. He cites Doug Rohrer's analysis of over 13,000 textbook problems showing only one in ten required retrieving material from earlier chapters, and a follow-up randomized trial showing interleaved, spaced practice significantly outperformed blocked chapter-end practice. Hendrick's central claim is that retrieval strength depends on curriculum design that builds 'return paths' back to hinge concepts, not on isolated teaching techniques performed on a Monday morning. He warns that visible activities like whiteboard quizzes can become 'pedagogical kayfabe' -- theater that looks like evidence-based teaching without producing real learning gains.
points: Rohrer's coding of 13,000+ US maths textbook problems found only about 10% required retrieving knowledge from a previous chapter, exposing how rarely curricula actually build in spaced return paths.

A randomized 50-classroom trial found interleaved, systematically-spaced practice outperformed standard end-of-chapter blocked practice by one of the largest effect sizes seen in this line of research.

Hendrick's key distinction: retrieval practice and spacing are curriculum-design properties, not teaching activities -- a five-minute starter quiz only works if it is timed against forgetting and points back to genuinely high-leverage knowledge.
Citing Christine Counsell, Hendrick warns that retrieval without a return path to bigger thematic ideas is 'an intransitive pedagogy, a pedagogy without an object.'
The strength of a memory effect scales with the effort required to retrieve it, meaning easy, frictionless 'what did we do yesterday' retrieval does almost nothing for long-term learning.
quotes: In the science of learning, the practice of retrieving previously learned material from memory is about the closest thing we have to penicillin in learning terms.

They have mutated from properties which exist to serve a curriculum into a range of techniques which give the impression of effective teaching but in reality, often grafted onto curricula never designed for them.

In 2020, Doug Rohrer and colleagues at the University of South Florida took several of the most used Maths textbooks in US schools and coded every problem (over 13,000 of them) against an ingenious question: does this practice problem require the student to retrieve anything from a previous chapter or does it just live inside the existing chapter?
For me, all this confirms the fact that the science of learning has far more to do with curriculum design than teaching activities.

A classroom full of kids raising mini-whiteboards like a Mexican wave might give the impression of learning but unless we examine closely what was being attended to then we risk the whole enterprise being pedagogical kayfabe.
To borrow again from Christine Counsell, retrieval practice without a destination or return path is an intransitive pedagogy, a pedagogy without an object.
The evidence never showed that quizzing strengthens memory per se; it showed that retrieval at a delay, timed against forgetting, strengthens memory.

Retconning the curriculum by bolting on the science of learning to materials that were never designed with them in mind might look evidence based but we will find out later if any learning actually took place, and probably too late.
